 134 | ## 3.1 Build primitives before frameworks
 135 | 
 136 | Initially avoid LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, or other agent

 139 | Implement these yourself:

 141 | ``` text

 144 | LLMResponse
 145 | Tool
 146 | ToolSchema
 147 | ToolRegistry
 148 | ToolExecutor
 149 | AgentState
 150 | AgentLoop
 151 | ContextManager
 152 | PermissionManager
 153 | ```
 154 | 
 155 | After understanding them, study frameworks and compare their

 158 | ## 3.2 Separate interfaces from implementations
 159 | 
 160 | The agent should depend on:
 161 | 
 162 | ``` text
 163 | LLMProvider
 164 | ```
 165 | 
 166 | rather than:
 167 | 
 168 | ``` text

 170 | ```

 187 | ## 3.3 Treat the model as an unreliable planner
 188 | 
 189 | The LLM can:
 190 | 
 191 | -   misunderstand a task
 192 | -   select the wrong tool
 193 | -   produce invalid arguments
 194 | -   hallucinate files
 195 | -   write incorrect code
 196 | -   stop before verification

 198 | Therefore every important action should be grounded by tools and real

 207 | step_id
 208 | timestamp
 209 | model
 210 | input tokens
 211 | output tokens
 212 | tool name
 213 | arguments
 214 | result
 215 | latency
 216 | exit code
 217 | error

 470 | # 7. Phase 1 --- LLM Provider Foundation
 471 | 
 472 | ## Objective
 473 | 
 474 | Understand an LLM API before building an agent.
 475 | 
 476 | Start with:
 477 | 
 478 | ``` text
 479 | User input
 480 |   ↓
 481 | Message
 482 |   ↓
 483 | Provider
 484 |   ↓
 485 | HTTP request
 486 |   ↓
 487 | Model
 488 |   ↓
 489 | HTTP response
 490 |   ↓
 491 | Normalized response
 492 | ```
 493 | 
 494 | ## `llm/base.py`
 495 | 
 496 | Use a small internal representation:
 497 | 
 498 | ``` python
 499 | from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
 500 | from dataclasses import dataclass
 501 | 
 502 | 
 503 | @dataclass
 504 | class Message:
 505 |     role: str
 506 |     content: str
 507 | 
 508 | 
 509 | @dataclass
 510 | class LLMResponse:
 511 |     content: str
 512 |     model: str | None = None
 513 | 
 514 | 
 515 | class LLMProvider(ABC):
 516 | 
 517 |     @abstractmethod
 518 |     async def chat(
 519 |         self,
 520 |         messages: list[Message],
 521 |     ) -> LLMResponse:
 522 |         raise NotImplementedError
 523 | ```
 524 | 
 525 | ### Why `dataclass`?
 526 | 
 527 | `Message` and `LLMResponse` are structured data containers.
 528 | 
 529 | Instead of repeatedly passing unstructured dictionaries:
 530 | 
 531 | ``` python
 532 | {"role": "user", "content": "hello"}
 533 | ```
 534 | 
 535 | you can use:
 536 | 
 537 | ``` python
 538 | Message(role="user", content="hello")
 539 | ```
 540 | 
 541 | The model objects can later grow to contain:
 542 | 
 543 | ``` text
 544 | Message
 545 | ├── role
 546 | ├── content
 547 | ├── tool_calls
 548 | ├── tool_call_id
 549 | └── metadata
 550 | ```
 551 | 
 552 | ### Why `ABC`?
 553 | 
 554 | `LLMProvider` defines a contract.
 555 | 
 556 | Every provider must implement:
 557 | 
 558 | ``` python
 559 | chat(messages)
 560 | ```
 561 | 
 562 | This allows:
 563 | 
 564 | ``` text
 565 | LLMProvider
 566 | ├── OpenRouterProvider
 567 | ├── OpenAIProvider
 568 | ├── AnthropicProvider
 569 | └── OllamaProvider
 570 | ```
 571 | 
 572 | without changing the agent.
 573 | 
 574 | `ABC` is not mandatory. `typing.Protocol` is another valid design. Use
 575 | `ABC` initially because it makes the interface/implementation
 576 | relationship explicit while learning.
 577 |

 580 | # 8. Phase 1.1 --- Raw API Communication

 592 | -   timeouts
 593 | -   response parsing

 596 | 
 597 | ``` text

 599 |

 601 | Authorization: Bearer <key>
 602 | Content-Type: application/json

 604 | Body:

 607 |   "messages": [...]

 712 | # 11. Phase 2 --- Tool Calling
 713 | 
 714 | This is the first major agent milestone.
 715 | 
 716 | ## Fundamental concept
 717 | 
 718 | A tool is an operation that the model can request but your application
 719 | executes.
 720 | 
 721 | Example:
 722 | 
 723 | ``` text
 724 | LLM:
 725 | I need to inspect main.py.
 726 | 
 727 | Tool call:
 728 | read_file
 729 | arguments:
 730 | {
 731 |   "path": "main.py"
 732 | }
 733 | ```
 734 | 
 735 | Your runtime:
 736 | 
 737 | ``` text
 738 | Tool call
 739 |    ↓
 740 | parse
 741 |    ↓
 742 | identify tool
 743 |    ↓
 744 | validate arguments
 745 |    ↓
 746 | permission check
 747 |    ↓
 748 | execute
 749 |    ↓
 750 | structured result
 751 |    ↓
 752 | append result to conversation
 753 |    ↓
 754 | LLM
 755 | ```
 756 | 
 757 | The model does not directly execute Python functions. Your runtime
 758 | interprets the model's request.

 762 | # 12. Tool Schema
 763 | 
 764 | Define each tool with:
 765 | 
 766 | ``` text
 767 | name
 768 | description
 769 | input schema
 770 | executor
 771 | permission requirements
 772 | ```
 773 | 
 774 | Example conceptual schema:
 775 | 
 776 | ``` json
 777 | {
 778 |   "name": "read_file",
 779 |   "description": "Read a UTF-8 text file from the workspace.",
 780 |   "parameters": {
 781 |     "type": "object",
 782 |     "properties": {
 783 |       "path": {
 784 |         "type": "string"
 785 |       }
 786 |     },
 787 |     "required": ["path"]
 788 |   }
 789 | }
 790 | ```
 791 | 
 792 | Use Pydantic to validate arguments internally.
 793 | 
 794 | For example:
 795 | 
 796 | ``` python
 797 | from pydantic import BaseModel
 798 | 
 799 | 
 800 | class ReadFileArgs(BaseModel):
 801 |     path: str
 802 | ```
 803 | 
 804 | If the model sends:
 805 | 
 806 | ``` json
 807 | {
 808 |   "path": 123
 809 | }
 810 | ```
 811 | 
 812 | the validation layer rejects or coerces it according to your configured
 813 | validation policy rather than letting malformed input reach the
 814 | filesystem.

 818 | # 13. Tool Registry
 819 | 
 820 | Do not write:
 821 | 
 822 | ``` python
 823 | if tool_name == "read_file":
 824 |     ...
 825 | elif tool_name == "write_file":
 826 |     ...
 827 | ```
 828 | 
 829 | Instead:
 830 | 
 831 | ``` text

 833 | ├── read_file
 834 | ├── write_file
 835 | ├── search_files
 836 | ├── apply_patch
 837 | ├── run_command
 838 | └── git
 839 | ```
 840 | 
 841 | Each registered tool provides:
 842 | 
 843 | ``` text
 844 | metadata
 845 | schema
 846 | validator
 847 | executor
 848 | policy
 849 | ```
 850 | 
 851 | This allows tools to be dynamically added and removed.

 855 | # 14. Tool Executor
 856 | 
 857 | Separate registry from execution.
 858 | 
 859 | ``` text
 860 | ToolRegistry
 861 |      ↓
 862 | find tool
 863 |      ↓
 864 | ToolExecutor
 865 |      ↓
 866 | validate
 867 |      ↓
 868 | authorize
 869 |      ↓
 870 | execute
 871 |      ↓
 872 | normalize result
 873 | ```
 874 | 
 875 | The executor should return structured observations.
 876 | 
 877 | Example shell result:
 878 | 
 879 | ``` json
 880 | {
 881 |   "exit_code": 1,
 882 |   "stdout": "...",
 883 |   "stderr": "AssertionError...",
 884 |   "duration_ms": 2310,
 885 |   "timed_out": false
 886 | }
 887 | ```
 888 | 
 889 | This is much better than returning a single text string because the
 890 | agent can reason over structured execution state.

1037 | # 19. Phase 5 --- The Agent Loop
1038 | 
1039 | Now combine the LLM and tools.
1040 | 
1041 | Basic loop:
1042 | 
1043 | ``` text
1044 | while task_not_complete:
1045 | 
1046 |     send current state to LLM
1047 | 
1048 |     if final response:
1049 |         stop
1050 | 
1051 |     if tool calls:
1052 |         for each tool call:
1053 |             validate
1054 |             authorize
1055 |             execute
1056 |             append observation
1057 | 
1058 |     increment iteration

1062 | 
1063 | ``` python
1064 | while not state.finished:
1065 | 
1066 |     response = await llm.chat(state.messages)
1067 | 
1068 |     if response.is_final:
1069 |         state.finished = True
1070 |         break
1071 | 
1072 |     for tool_call in response.tool_calls:
1073 |         result = await executor.execute(tool_call)
1074 |         state.add_observation(result)
1075 | ```

1224 | # 23. Repository-Aware Retrieval Architecture
1225 | 
1226 | ``` text
1227 | Repository
1228 |     ↓
1229 | Scanner
1230 |     ↓
1231 | Ignore rules
1232 |     ↓
1233 | File metadata
1234 |     ↓
1235 | Chunking
1236 |     ↓

1238 | │ lexical index │ symbol index    │ vector index    │
1239 | │ ripgrep/BM25  │ Tree-sitter     │ embeddings      │
1240 | └───────────────┴─────────────────┴─────────────────┘
1241 |                        ↓
1242 |                  Query analysis
1243 |                        ↓
1244 |                 Hybrid retrieval
1245 |                        ↓
1246 |                    Reranking
1247 |                        ↓
1248 |                  Context budget
1249 |                        ↓

1254 | 
1255 | # 24. Why Hybrid Retrieval?
1256 | 
1257 | Code search benefits from exact matches and semantic similarity.
1258 | 
1259 | Example:
1260 | 
1261 | User asks:
1262 | 
1263 | ``` text
1264 | Where is user authentication handled?
1265 | ```
1266 | 
1267 | Exact search can find:
1268 | 
1269 | ``` text
1270 | authenticate
1271 | login
1272 | JWT
1273 | middleware
1274 | ```
1275 | 
1276 | Semantic retrieval can find code that performs authentication without
1277 | using the exact word.
1278 | 
1279 | Tree-sitter can identify:
1280 | 
1281 | ``` text
1282 | class AuthMiddleware
1283 | function validate_token
1284 | function login
1285 | ```
1286 | 
1287 | Combining these signals is usually more useful than relying on only one
1288 | retrieval method.

1459 | ``` text

 240 |     async def count_tokens(self, messages: List[Message]) -> int:
 241 |         """
 242 |         Estimate token count for input messages.
 243 |         Default naive implementation based on word count; providers should override.
 244 |         """
 245 |         total_words = 0
 246 |         for msg in messages:
 247 |             if isinstance(msg.content, str):
 248 |                 total_words += len(msg.content.split())
 249 |             elif isinstance(msg.content, list):
 250 |                 for part in msg.content:
 251 |                     if isinstance(part, dict) and "text" in part:
 252 |                         total_words += len(part["text"].split())
 253 |         return int(total_words * 1.33)
